reference_spans.exact_text: INTRODUCTION: Lactate is a key biomarker in the assessment of sepsis, reflecting tissue hypoperfusion and correlating with disease severity and outcomes.
However, reliance on standard laboratory testing may delay clinical decision-making in time-sensitive situations.
Point-of-care (POC) lactate testing provides rapid bedside assessment, potentially facilitating earlier risk stratification and intervention.
This study aimed to evaluate the predictive value of POC lactate for pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission and mortality in pediatric patients with sepsis.

METHODS: This was a retrospective observational study of children aged 3 months to 14 years presenting to the pediatric emergency department in a tertiary care children's hospital with a diagnosis of sepsis.
Data were extracted from electronic medical records.
RESULTS: A total of 149 pediatric patients with sepsis were included, of whom 90 underwent POC lactate testing.
Elevated POC lactate levels were observed in 38.9% of tested patients.
Elevated POC lactate was significantly associated with PICU admission, as well as the need for mechanical ventilation and inotropic support.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated modest but statistically significant predictive performance for PICU admission (AUC = 0.641), whereas no predictive value was observed for mortality (AUC = 0.544).

CONCLUSIONS: Point-of-care lactate may serve as a practical supplementary biomarker that can facilitate early risk stratification by identifying children with sepsis at increased risk of PICU admission and requiring advanced interventions.

Nevertheless, its modest discriminatory performance necessitates interpretation in conjunction with clinical assessment and additional biomarkers rather than as an independent predictor of sepsis severity.

reference_spans.exact_text: INTRODUCTION: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly among young children and older adults.
Bacterial pathogens account for a substantial proportion of CAP cases, yet early identification of bacteremia and etiologic agents remains challenging.
Blood cultures are slow and often have a limited clinical impact.
We hypothesized that plasma metabolomics can capture systemic metabolic signatures associated with blood culture positivity and bacterial etiology at the time of hospital admission.
METHODS: Plasma samples from 80 patients with bacterial CAP (40 culture-positive and 40 age- and sex-matched culture-negative) were collected on the first day of admission.
Metabolomic profiling was performed using complementary platforms, including untargeted 1H-NMR, GC-MS, and targeted LC-DIMS/MS.
Multivariate and univariate analyses were applied to identify discriminating metabolic features.
RESULTS: Distinct metabolic phenotypes were observed between culture-positive and culture-negative patients across all platforms.
OPLS-DA models demonstrated significant discrimination, with GC-MS and 1H-NMR showing strong internally cross-validated discriminatory performance (Q2 > 0.45, AUROC > 0.90).

Culture-positive CAP was characterized by increased phenylalanine, urea, and mannose, alongside decreased amino acids and fatty acids, indicating coordinated alterations in nitrogen metabolism, energy pathways, and lipid remodeling.
CONCLUSIONS: Plasma metabolomics identified distinct systemic metabolic patterns associated with blood culture positivity and, in exploratory analysis, with S. pneumoniae etiology.

These discovery-stage findings demonstrate reproducible systemic metabolic patterns associated with blood culture positivity and bacterial etiology and support further validation of targeted metabolite signatures in independent CAP cohorts.

cases.question: What design was used in the Canadian vaccine perception study?

reference_spans.exact_text: OBJECTIVE: Vaccination has been scientifically proven to be safe and to prevent infectious diseases.
The COVID-19 vaccine has been crucial in combating the pandemic.
In Canada, despite widespread vaccine hesitancy, little has specifically addressed older adults from racialized communities.
This study investigates perceptions of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness among older adults by racial background, examining the influence of major racial discrimination and health literacy.
STUDY DESIGN: A cross-sectional pan-Canadian study.
METHODS: Data were collected using Computer-Assisted Web Interviewing (March 2025).
The COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness was tested with t-tests, ANOVA, and multivariable linear regression.
RESULTS: 581 participants were included: Arab (11.5%), Asian (15.8%), Black (16.2%), Indigenous (9%), and White (35.8%); including men (48.2%), women (43.0%), and 8.8% identifying as non-binary.
Participants 65 years and above reported significantly greater perceived COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness versus 55-64 years old (t(579) = 2.17, p = .015)).
Asian and White participants were more likely to have a good perception of COVID-19 vaccines versus Black and Indigenous (F(6,574) = 2.88, p = .009) participants.
CONCLUSIONS: Perceptions of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness among 55+ in Canada varied substantially across racial groups, with differences linked to experiences of discrimination and literacy levels.

These findings highlight the need for targeted, equity-oriented public health strategies that address both structural racism and misinformation to improve vaccine confidence among older adults in marginalized communities.
